Understanding the different operating principles one can easily see what the processor will do or not do in certain situations. This becomes very important for troubleshooting purposes.
You know that the processor operates in one of two modes, user or supervisor. The processor also operates within one of three states, which are: normal, exception, and halted.
EXCEPTION
SUPERVISOR
Let's look at what these states mean with regard to the processor operation.
Let's begin the lesson on OPERATION OF THE 68000..........................
LESSON MENU
As the name implies, the normal state is where the normal program operation occurs. This state can occur in both user and supervisor modes.
DISCUSSION
The exception state only occurs in supervisor mode. However, programs operating in user mode can cause the processor to switch to supervisor mode. This switching is caused by exceptions.
An exception is the occurrence of a condition outside normal operation. For example, trying to divide by zero or accessing an illegal address would be considered an exception.

Interrupts are also classified as exceptions. When exceptions occur, the handling of the exception is performed in the supervisor mode. Switching of modes automatically occurs within the microprocessor.
Later in this lesson, when we discuss exceptions, you will have a better understanding of the exception state.

The halted state occurs only in the supervisor mode. This state is entered when a certain sequence of exceptions occur. The processor can only continue based on signals input to the system, like: interrupts, or reset. As the name implies, the system is halted.

The states of operation are important in understanding exactly what the processor is doing. Certain operations perform differently in different states. Even certain input signals will provide different types of information to the system.
Also vital to a 68000 system are the vector addresses and exceptions. Since these two topics are so closely related, they will be discussed together.

When exceptions occur, the microprocessor needs to operate based on the exception. A vector table located within the memory will indicate to the microprocessor what address to execute code at based on a specific exception.

Each exception is assigned a vector number, for example an address error is vector number 3. To get the vector address, or actual memory location that the vector number represents, multiply the vector number by 4. This results in the address of 0Ch.
At this location, a long word address value is stored that is loaded into the program counter if an address error occurs. The table below shows the vector table.

Exceptions are organized into three groups: 0, 1 and 2. Group 0 has the highest priority whereas group 2 has the lowest. The table below shows which exceptions are in which group. Let's look at each of the exceptions and what happens in the system during each one.
CATION LABELS
EXCEPTIONS

The priority of the exceptions determines which exceptions will be processed first. For example, if an Interrupt occurred and then a Bus Error occurred, the Bus Error would be handled before the Interrupt is finished being handled.
However, if a Bus Error occurred, and then an interrupt occurred, the interrupt wouldn't be recognized because it has a lower priority.
The reset exception is different from the other exceptions. In this exception, the system is set to supervisor mode and reinitialized. Initialization will be covered later in this lesson.

A bus error occurs when the bus error pin of the processor is set too low. This indicates that something external to the microprocessor is not working properly. When this exception occurs, the following steps are performed by the microprocessor:
1. The contents of the status register is saved to an internal register.
2. The Supervisor bit of the status register is set to 1 and the Trace bit is set to 0. This sets trace off and puts the processor into the supervisor mode.
3. The following information is pushed to the stack in this order:
1. Program counter low 2. Program counter high
3. Internally saved status register 4. Instruction register
5. Access Address Low 6. Access Address High

4. The vector number for a bus error is 2. This value is multiplied by four yielding the vector address value of 08h. The long word size data located at location 08h is then placed in the program counter. Remember, the program counter value is where the processor will get its next instruction.

The status information word contains a bit indicating if the processor was reading or writing, whether the error occurred accessing an instruction or data, and the function code of the processor when the error occurred. -

The information saved to the stack with this type of exception is not normally used to continue executing code after the exception has been processed. Normally this information will aid in determining where the error occurred.

You will see in many of the other exceptions how you can recover from an exception and continue with normal code execution. The access address is the address on the address bus when the exception occurred.
This value is more meaningful in the Illegal Address exception. Remember, the bus error indicates a problem in an external circuit.

An illegal address occurs when either an instruction is on an odd address or you try accessing word or long word size data on an odd address. Remember, there is an address limitation to where word and long word size information can be stored, only on even address.
CATION LABELS

When an Illegal Address exception occurs, the same exact steps followed by a Bus Error are performed, except for the vector number which is 3, yielding a vector address of 0Ch. Again, recovery from an address error is not normally performed.

The information on the stack can be used by a technician to locate and solve code problems. The Access Address will contain either the address of the instruction that is located on an illegal address, or the illegal address an instruction is trying to access word or long word data at.

The status word, the last word of information pushed to the stack, will indicate whether the error occurred from an instruction or data on an illegal address. The graphic below shows the configuration of the status word and how each of the bits can be decoded.
You have now seen all of the exceptions from group 0. None of the other exceptions push a status word to the stack. Remember, group 0 exceptions have the highest priority.

The Trace exception is used for debugging code currently being executed. After each instruction is executed in a program, the trace exception is called and normal information about the registers is displayed on the screen.
The trace mode feature is turned on by setting the trace bit to high. The following actions are performed after an instruction has executed with the trace bit set to 1.
1. The contents of the status register is saved to an internal register.
2. The Supervisor bit of the status register is set to 1 and the Trace bit is set to 0. This sets trace the trace mode off and puts the processor in the supervisor mode.
3. The vector number is determined based on the exception, in this case 9.
4. The program counter and the internally saved status register are pushed to the stack.
5. The vector address is calculated, 4 x 9 yielding 24h. The value stored at this location is placed in the program counter.
6. Execution begins at the value in the program counter.

7. After the exception code is finished, the RTE instruction can be used to "ReTurn from Exception." This takes the program counter and status register off of the stack and loads them into their associated registers.ters.registers.egisters.........ext instruction.

You have probably noticed that this exception does have some similarities to the other exceptions we have talked about. Notice that the trace bit is set to 0 when the trace occurs. This is necessary so that the trace exception code can execute properly.
If the bit wasn't set to zero, the trace exception would be called again after the first instruction of the exception, and this would happen over and over again.

Normally, in the trace exception code, the contents of the registers is displayed and maybe an option to perform the next instruction. When you want to return to the next instruction in your code, the RTE instruction loads the original value of the status register back into the status register, and the program counter, which was incremented to the next instruction.

Remember, before you changed the trace bit to 0 you saved the original copy of the status register. This value had the trace bit set to 1. Thus, your next line of code will be evaluated and the trace exception called again.

The only way to disable the trace is to modify the original value of the status register that is stored on the stack while in the exception. The trace exception will be used in the lesson involving the debugging of code.
You have seen a hardware oriented description of the interrupts. In this section we will focus on the internal handling of interrupts. Recall the interrupt mask of the status register.

If an interrupt occurs with a value below that of the interrupt mask, it will be ignored. Otherwise the following steps occur.
1. Save the status register to an internal register.

2. Set the status register supervisor bit to 1, trace 0, and put the value of the interrupt in the interrupt mask bits. This places the processor in the supervisor mode, turns trace off (if on), and keep interrupts of a lower priority from being processed.
3. The value of the interrupt is placed on the address lines A1, A2, and A3. Also, all three function code lines of the processor are set to high.

These signals from the processor are decoded by external devices and a timer, known as a watch dog timer. This timer prevents the system from waiting forever for devices to indicate to the processor that they have caused the interrupt.
One of three conditions will occur; the timer will run out setting the bus error pin to low, a device will set the data acknowledge pin to low, or a device will set the valid peripheral pin to low.
The three pins used within the interrupt exception do not operate as previously mentioned. These three pins now indicate the type of interrupt.
Let's look at what happens in each of these three interrupt conditions. When the watch dog timer elapses and the bus error pin is set to low, this indicates that a spurious interrupt has occurred.
A spurious interrupt means that a false interrupt was acknowledged from some external device. When this occurs the following steps are performed by the system:
4. Vector 18 x 4 = address 60 (see vector chart) determined.
5. The Program Counter and internally saved status register are pushed to the stack.
6. The value at the vector address is placed into program counter and program execution begins at a new location.
7. RTE will return processing where it left off before the exception occurred, provided that the stack is correct after the exception program.

If the data acknowledge pin is set to low [which also should be connected to the watch dog timer to prevent it from finishing], then a user vector condition should occur. If this signal is set, the processor will read from the data lines a value indicating which user interrupt vector to use.

This value must be placed on the data lines before the data acknowledge signal is set low. This type of interrupt is used for devices specifically designed to operate with the 68000 which can indicate many different types of interrupts.
The following additional steps are performed for a user interrupt:

4. (Vector Fh + user interrupt value) * 4. The user interrupt values that will be accepted from the data lines are 31h to F0h. Any other value will cause value zero to be added, which results in vector F (or 15) known as the uninitialized interrupt.
5. The Program Counter and internally saved status register are pushed to the stack.
6. The value at the vector address is placed into program counter and program execution begins at a new location.
7. RTE will return processing where it left off before the exception occurred, provided that the stack is correct after the exception program.

The last type of interrupt is the autovector interrupt. This is when the valid peripheral address pin is set to low and the watch dog timer is disabled. This type of interrupt is for devices not specifically designed to work with the 68000.
1. Save the status register to an internal register.

2. Set the status register supervisor bit to 1, trace 0, and put the value of the interrupt in the interrupt mask bits. This places the processor in the supervisor mode, turns trace off (if on), and keep interrupts of a lower priority from being processed.
3. The value of the interrupt is placed on the address lines A1, A2, and A3. Also, all three function code lines of the processor are set to high.

The value of the interrupt is added to 18 (12h) to determine the vector number. The vector chart shows where each of the vectors are. The following additional steps are performed for an autovector interrupt:
5. The Program Counter and internally saved status register are pushed to the stack.
6. The value at the vector address is placed into program counter and program execution begins at a new location.
7. RTE will return processing where it left off before the exception occurred, provided that the stack is correct after the exception program.
While some of this information may seem a bit overwhelming, don't worry, as you work more and more with the 68000 you will gradually understand the operation of the exceptions better.

There are a few important notes to realize about the interrupt exception. In the user mode, the interrupt value on the interrupt pins of the processor is used for priority purposes, this value is not used to determine the actual vector to use..
In the autovector mode, the interrupt value is used for both priority and vector number. It's very limited compared to the user interrupts, however, easier to implement into the system.

A spurious interrupt could occur if a device actually calls an interrupt and a bus error occurs before the data acknowledge or valid peripheral address pins could be asserted. If a spurious interrupt occurs, you may need to check and see if a bus error really did occur.
Interrupts are very important in a system. You may recall the earlier discussion on interrupts which gave examples of devices which operate primarily with interrupting the system, like a mouse.

A privilege violation occurs when a user program tries to use an instruction that can only be used in the supervisor mode. The following list of instructions, when used in the user mode, will cause a privilege violation:
STOP, RESET, MOVE to SR, ANDI to SR, ORI to SR, EORI to SR,
MOVE USP to A(n), MOVE to USP and RTEEEEEEE Illegal Address
When a privilege violation occurs, the following steps are performed by the microprocessor:
1. The contents of the status register is saved to an internal register.
2. The Supervisor bit of the status register is set to 1 and the Trace bit is set to 0. This sets trace the trace mode off and puts the processor in the supervisor mode.
3. The vector number is determined based on the exception, in this case 8.
4. The program counter and the internally saved status register are pushed to the stack.
5. The vector address is calculated. The value stored at this location is placed in the program counter.
6. Execution begins at the value in the program counter.

The privilege violation exception is important because it prevents user programs from performing unauthorized operations. The privilege violation exception is the last of the group 1 exceptions.

The trap violation occurs when the TRAP instruction is used. The TRAP instruction allows the user to execute one of 16 segments of code assigned to a trap value.
When this instruction is executed, it contains a value from 0h to 15h. This value is then added to 20h to determine the vector number. Then, the code is run and you can return to where you left off.

This is kind of like a hard coded subroutine. You may remember traps used in earlier programs you entered to clear the display or reposition the cursor. These were routines that would be run over and over, thus making them a good candidate to be placed in an easy to use trap. The steps below show what happens when a program calls a TRAP exception:
1. The status register is saved to an internal register.
2. The Supervisor bit of the status register is set to 1 and the Trace bit is set to 0. This sets trace the trace mode off and puts the processor in the supervisor mode.
3. The vector number is determined based on the exception, 20h + Trap #.
4. The program counter and the internally saved status register are pushed to the stack.
5. The vector address is calculated. The value stored at this location is placed in the program counter.
6. Execution begins at the value in the program counter.

7. After the exception code is finished, the RTE instruction can be used to "ReTurn from Exception." This takes the program counter and status register off of the stack and loads them into their associated registers.s.ers.d registers.s..sociated registers.sters.registers.egisters.........ext instruction.

The CHK exception, known as the check Register against bounds, is used to determine if a data register value is within a certain range. In some cases, this is used when checking memory being accessed.

If you only had 1k of RAM attached to a computer, you could check a value that you are going to use as an address to make sure that it is within the 1k value. The syntax for this instruction is CHK <EA>, <Dn>.

Now you have seen all of the exceptions that can occur in the 68000 microprocessor system. You can see that there are many similarities between the different exceptions. Exceptions are important because, in most cases, they prevent errors from going undetected.

Microprocessors don't make mistakes and, if they do, the same mistake will occur over and over due to a defect in the processor. However, processors are tested heavily, leaving most errors traceable to human usage.
If, in your career, you do a lot of microprocessor work, you will be thankful for exceptions.
